title: Apollo 11 Lunar Landing Mission Press Kit — curated evaluation excerpt

pages.text: The United States will launch a three-man spacecraft toward the Moon on July 16 with the goal of landing two astronaut-explorers on the lunar surface four days later. The mission is called Apollo 11.

A plaque fastened to the descent stage of the lunar module bears a map of Earth and the inscription: Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969 A.D. We came in peace for all mankind. Armstrong and Aldrin will also emplant an American flag on the lunar surface.

The prime mission objective of Apollo 11 is: Perform a manned lunar landing and return. Successful fulfillment will meet the national goal set by President Kennedy on May 25, 1961. Neil Armstrong is commander, Michael Collins is command module pilot, and Edwin Aldrin is lunar module pilot.

The backup crew helps the prime crew with mission preparation and hardware checkout. They receive nearly complete mission training as a foundation for later assignment, and they are prepared to fly if the prime crew becomes unavailable.

Leftover liquid propellant in the Saturn third stage will be vented through the engine bell to place the stage on a slingshot trajectory that misses the Moon and enters solar orbit. During translunar coast Apollo 11 uses passive thermal control, rotating slowly about its roll axis.

After touchdown the landing crew prepares the lunar module for immediate ascent and rests before depressurizing for a two-man EVA. Armstrong steps onto the lunar surface first, followed by Aldrin about 40 minutes later. Their planned surface activity lasts two hours and 40 minutes.

Four basic maneuvers using the lunar module maneuvering and attitude thrusters bring the lunar module and command module together for docking about three and a half hours after liftoff from the Moon. The boost out of lunar orbit for the return journey is planned for about 135 hours after Earth liftoff.

During the transearth coast Apollo 11 again controls solar heat loads with the passive thermal control barbecue technique. Three transearth midcourse corrections are possible and will be planned in real time to adjust the Earth entry corridor.

The Apollo 11 countdown starts at T minus 28 hours, with a six-hour built-in hold planned at T minus 9 hours before launch vehicle propellant loading. Pre-count operations begin about five days before launch.
The final countdown schedule calls for ignition sequence start at T minus 8.9 seconds, all engines running at T minus 2 seconds, and liftoff at T zero.
The mission events table schedules lunar module touchdown at 102 hours, 47 minutes, 11 seconds ground elapsed time. Depressurization for lunar surface EVA is scheduled at 112 hours, 30 minutes.

Apollo 11 will launch from Kennedy Space Center Launch Complex 39A. The launch azimuth can vary from 72 degrees to 106 degrees. Trajectory information assumes a July 16 launch and may change before or during the mission.
